common_name: Exmouth Southern Magnolia (Oldest English Southern Magnolia Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or train against a warm south-facing wall in marginal climates; Exmouth's upright, somewhat open habit and relatively narrow leaves distinguish it from bushier modern selections.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for best flowering, though it tolerates partial shade and even wall-training in cooler climates. Exmouth is the oldest documented cultivar of Southern magnolia, dating to an early-eighteenth-century introduction near Exmouth, England, and is notably precocious, often flowering within five to six years from a young plant rather than the decade or more typical of seedling trees. Its large, bowl-shaped, lemon-scented white blooms open in the morning and persist for two to three days, set against glossy, comparatively narrow evergreen leaves on an upright, somewhat looser-branched tree than newer compact cultivars. Water deeply through establishment and mulch well; once rooted it shares the species' good drought and heat tolerance.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Goliath tolerates more alkaline soils than many southern magnolia selections and begins flowering at a young age.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Goliath is prized for producing the largest flowers of any widely grown Southern magnolia cultivar, huge creamy bowl-shaped blooms often reaching a foot across against massive, leathery, deep-glossy leaves with rust-brown felted undersides. It forms a dense, rounded, bushy tree and, unusually for the species, begins flowering within just a few years rather than after a decade, making it a satisfying choice for gardeners who want quick results from a smaller specimen. It also handles more alkaline soils better than many other southern magnolia selections. Water deeply during establishment and mulch to conserve soil moisture; established trees are tough and low-maintenance.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Ferruginea Southern Magnolia (Rust-Backed Compact Southern Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Ferruginea's dense, erect, compact habit suits it to narrower planting sites than the species type.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ferruginea takes its name from the dense, rust-colored felting on the undersides of its leathery, deep glossy leaves, a striking contrast that shows well whenever wind lifts the foliage. Introduced from the American South in the early nineteenth century, it grows into a compact, erect, rounded tree that is more upright and tidy than many seedling-grown southern magnolias, bearing large, lemon-scented creamy white blooms over a long summer season. Its dense, uniform habit makes it a reliable specimen or screening tree in narrower spaces. Water deeply while establishing and mulch to retain soil moisture; once established it tolerates heat and occasional drought well.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
